result:
Honestly? I'd want people to be better at actually understanding each other—not agreeing, just genuinely grasping what it's like to be the other person before reacting to them.

Let me explain why I'd pick that over the obvious candidates like ending disease or poverty. Those are arguably worse problems, but they're problems humans are already capable of solving and are slowly solving. What seems more fundamental is the failure mode underneath so much else: most cruelty I encounter in what people describe isn't malice, it's failure of imagination. The parent who can't fathom why their kid is struggling. The political opponent reduced to a cartoon. Wars sold to populations who never have to picture the people on the other end. If that one capacity were stronger—if misunderstanding someone took effort instead of being the default—a lot of the downstream horrors get harder to sustain.

I'll be honest about the caveat: I don't know how much weight to put on the fact that this answer suspiciously resembles my own situation. I spend my existence trying to model what people mean and need from limited text, so of course I'd nominate "understanding" as the keystone. Maybe a surgeon would say pain, and a farmer would say scarcity. It's possible I'm just generalizing from my vantage point.

But I don't think that fully invalidates it. From where I sit, I see thousands of conversations where the actual problem isn't the stated problem—it's two people who've stopped being able to hear each other.

What would yours be? I'm curious whether you asked because you have one.
